perfeito - veja só qual foi o pedido que eu fiz ao v0, foi esse prompt mais esse deep research. analise a codebase e veja o que falta ser feito ainda
Worked for 3m 39s

Sim — a leitura geral é: o v0 começou o projeto, mas entregou um bootstrap parcial, não uma implementação próxima do prompt. Eu classificaria como algo entre Phase 1 parcial + Phase 2 muito reduzida + começo da Phase 3, com risco alto de nem compilar ainda.

O pedido original era um Flutter desktop-first ASW Observatory, com design system atômico primeiro, mock workspace em .md com frontmatter, data layer, shell, Map/Operate/History/Governance/Asset Detail, e visual “ultradark obsidian glass”. Esse contrato vem diretamente do prompt e do deep research. 

prompt

 

research

Diagnóstico curto

O que existe:

pubspec.yaml está configurado como Flutter e inclui dependências coerentes com o pedido: go_router, flutter_riverpod, yaml, graphview, fl_chart, collection, intl. 

pubspec

Há uma tentativa de Design System com tokens, atoms, molecules, organisms e templates exportados. 

design_system

Há tokens visuais bons para a direção “obsidian glass”: fundos near-black, cyan/violet/gold accents, status colors, canonicality colors, lane colors e asset colors. 

ds_colors

 

ds_colors

Há modelos de domínio para Agent, Skill, Workflow, Task, ChangelogEntry e AssetEdge. 

models

 

models

Há um parser inicial para YAML de agent/skill/workflow e parser simples de changelog markdown. 

workspace_parser

 

workspace_parser

Há alguns mocks: 5 agents, 4 skills, 3 workflows, 1 fila de tasks e 5 changelogs, conforme o PR que adicionou 20 arquivos. 

Initialize ASW Observatory with…

O que está errado/insuficiente:

Não encontrei lib/main.dart, lib/app/app.dart, lib/app/router.dart nem feature screens óbvias. Então, do jeito que está, parece faltar a aplicação Flutter propriamente dita.

O README ainda é o boilerplate de Next.js/v0, mandando rodar npm run dev e editar app/page.tsx, o que contradiz o pubspec.yaml Flutter. 

README

 

README

O pubspec.yaml declara assets em assets/mock_workspace/..., mas os mocks que encontrei estão em mock_workspace/..., fora da árvore declarada. 

pubspec

O prompt exigia .md com YAML frontmatter; os agentes/skills/workflows implementados são .yaml puro, sem frontmatter. Exemplo: mock_workspace/.opencode/orchestrator/agent.yaml. 

agent

O prompt exigia pelo menos 20 tasks espalhadas em 5 lanes; o repo tem uma fila única com 6 tasks em um arquivo mock_workspace/.opencode/tasks/queue.md, e não os diretórios docs/tasks/00-planning etc. 

queue

O prompt exigia pelo menos 12 changelog entries com frontmatter; o repo tem 5 changelogs e o exemplo lido não tem frontmatter, só markdown por seção. 

2025-06-01-coder-update

O modelo não segue o backbone pedido. O prompt pedia AssetKind, EdgeKind, Canonicality, WorkspaceAsset, WorkspaceEdge; o repo criou um modelo mais genérico com AssetType { agent, skill, workflow, task, doc }, sem subskill, changelog, script, reference, rule, nem Canonicality. 

models

O parser não extrai frontmatter do padrão pedido; ele parseia YAML inteiro para agents/skills/workflows e o changelog por headings, não pelo frontmatter id/date/project/task/type/impact/skills. 

workspace_parser

 

workspace_parser

Problema mais grave: há sinais fortes de que não compila

Tem inconsistências de nomes entre componentes/tokens/templates:

DSColors existe com DS maiúsculo. 

ds_colors


Mas ds_graph_canvas.dart usa DsColors, além de propriedades que não existem no token mostrado, como accentGreen, accentAmber, neutral500, background, surface, border. 

ds_graph_canvas

 

ds_graph_canvas

DSMotion existe. 

ds_motion


Mas o graph usa DsMotion.fast. 

ds_graph_canvas

DSShell existe e recebe content, não body. 

ds_shell


Mas MasterDetailTemplate chama DsShell(... body: ...), com classe e parâmetro divergentes. 

master_detail_template

DSSidebar existe com DSSidebarItem, selectedId, onItemTap, expanded. 

ds_sidebar


Mas o template usa SidebarItem, DsSidebar, selectedIndex, onItemSelected, isCollapsed. 

master_detail_template

 

master_detail_template

DSTopbar existe, mas recebe searchBar/showSearch; o template chama DsTopbar com searchQuery, onSearchChanged, filters, selectedFilters, onFiltersChanged. 

ds_topbar

 

master_detail_template

Então a prioridade zero é fazer o projeto compilar antes de continuar produto.

Gap report por fase do prompt
Fase	Estado	O que falta
Phase 1 — Atomic Design System	Parcial	Normalizar nomes DS* vs Ds*; corrigir APIs entre atoms/molecules/organisms/templates; criar gallery route; validar acessibilidade/focus states; garantir que todos os exports resolvem.
Phase 2 — Mock Workspace	Muito incompleto	Mover para assets/mock_workspace; trocar .yaml puro por .md com YAML frontmatter; criar agents exigidos, 13 skills/super-skills com SKILL.md, sub-skills/workflows/references/scripts; 11 workflows; 20 tasks em 5 lanes; 12 changelogs.
Phase 3 — Data Layer	Esqueleto	Criar parser de frontmatter markdown; parser de tasks; parser de skill hierarchy; repository/service; normalized graph com WorkspaceAsset, WorkspaceEdge, AssetKind, EdgeKind, Canonicality; diagnósticos de governança.
Phase 4 — Product Shell	Ausente ou não localizado	main.dart, app root, router, Riverpod providers, dashboard/overview, layout desktop com rail + inspector.
Phase 5 — Feature Screens	Ausente ou não localizado	Map, Operate, History, Governance, Asset Detail universal; search/filter; graph modes; task detail; changelog impact path.
Phase 6 — Polish	Não começou	Responsividade real, storytelling panels, empty/loading/error states, keyboard navigation, visual polish, demo coherence.
Próxima ordem correta de trabalho

# Mock Workspace Corpus Contract

> **Task**: 0001 — Mock Workspace Contract Baseline
> **EPIC**: 02 — Warp Prism Mock Workspace Corpus
> **Status**: APPROVED
> **Date**: 2026-06-07

---

## 1. Objective

Define the migration contract for replacing the legacy `mock_workspace/` YAML corpus with a markdown-frontmatter corpus under `assets/mock_workspace/`.

---

## 2. Required counts

| Asset kind    | Minimum count | Source in prompt.txt            |
|---------------|---------------|---------------------------------|
| Agents        | 9             | "Required mock agents" section  |
| Skills        | 13            | "Required mock skills" section  |
| Workflows     | 11            | "Required mock workflows" section |
| Tasks         | 20            | "Required mock tasks" section   |
| Changelog entries | 12        | "Required mock changelog entries" section |

---

## 3. Required agents (9)

```
architect-orchestrator.md
builder-orchestrator.md
reviewer-orchestrator.md
gt-harness-architect.md
gt-code-quality-reviewer.md
gt-security-reviewer.md
gt-external-intelligence-analyst.md
gt-task-architect.md
gt-wave-orchestrator.md
```

Location: `assets/mock_workspace/.opencode/agents/<name>.md`

Each agent `.md` file must have YAML frontmatter with at minimum:
- `name`, `model` (provider/name), `mode`, `description`, `skills` (list), `workflows` (list)

---

## 4. Required skills (13)

```
harness-architecture/
project-management/
development-methodologies/
code-quality-harness/
coding-execution-harness/
agent-wiki/
indexing-skills/
external-intelligence/
frontend-quality-harness/
design-system-harness/
browser-harness/
remediation-harness/
agent-cli-delegation/
```

Location: `assets/mock_workspace/.opencode/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md`

Each SKILL.md must have YAML frontmatter with at minimum:
- `name`, `description`, `triggers` (list), `sub_skills` (list), `canonicality`, `tags` (list)

Each super-skill directory should contain:
- `SKILL.md`, `sub-skills/`, `workflows/`, `references/`, `scripts/`

---

## 5. Required workflows (11)

```
gt-ganthritor-onboard.md
architect-orchestration.md
builder-orchestration.md
reviewer-orchestration.md
gt-create-tasks.md
plan-evidence-to-tasks.md
audit-tasks.md
gt-harness-architecture.md
gt-code-review.md
gt-verify-task-completion.md
gt-research-orchestration.md
```

Location: `assets/mock_workspace/.opencode/workflows/<name>.md`

Each workflow `.md` file must have YAML frontmatter with at minimum:

## 9. Parser deltas and model deltas for EPIC 03

### 9.1 Current state (models.dart)

| Aspect | Current value |
|--------|--------------|
| Backbone enum | `AssetType { agent, skill, workflow, task, doc }` |
| Edge model | `AssetEdge { sourceId, targetId, edgeType: String }` — freeform string type |
| Canonicality | Not modeled |
| Base class | `Asset` with `id, name, description, version, createdAt, updatedAt, tags, metadata` |
| Agent model | Rich: status, model, systemPrompt, capabilities, tools, skillIds, workflowIds |
| Skill model | Has inputs/outputs/steps (pipeline-oriented), usedByAgentIds |
| Workflow model | Has trigger, stages, errorHandling, avgDurationMinutes, successRate |
| Task model | Has status, priority, assignedAgentId, workflowId, startedAt, completedAt, progress |
| Changelog model | Has summary, changes (ChangeSection), affectedAssets, evidence, author |
| Frontmatter | Not parsed; files are pure YAML or heading-based markdown |

### 9.2 Target state (prompt.txt contract)

| Aspect | Target value |
|--------|-------------|
| Backbone enum | `AssetKind { agent, skill, subskill, workflow, task, changelog, script, reference, rule }` |
| Edge enum | `EdgeKind { contains, routesTo, dependsOn, references, changedBy, proves, uses }` |
| Canonicality enum | `{ parentCanonical, childLocal, generated, appendOnly, archive, mock }` |
| Base class | `WorkspaceAsset { id, kind, name, path, description, canonicality, frontmatter, tags, triggers, edges }` |
| Edge class | `WorkspaceEdge` (graph-normalized) |
| Agent model | Flat frontmatter: name, model (string), mode, description, skills (list), workflows (list) |
| Skill model | Frontmatter: name, description, triggers, sub_skills, canonicality, tags; body is markdown |
| Workflow model | Frontmatter: name, description, uses_skills, kind; body is markdown |
| Task model | Frontmatter: id, title, status, priority, owner, created, updated, skills, workflows, depends_on, proof_state, review_score; body is markdown with Goal/Scope/Exit Conditions/Verification Commands/Completion Evidence |
| Changelog model | Frontmatter: id, date, project, task, type, impact, skills; body is markdown with Why/Changed/Evidence |
| Frontmatter | YAML frontmatter delimited by `---` at top of every `.md` file |

### 9.3 Required parser changes (EPIC 03)

1. **Frontmatter extraction**: New `parseFrontmatter(String content)` that splits on `---` delimiters and returns `(Map<String, dynamic> frontmatter, String body)`.

2. **Agent parser rewrite**: Replace `parseAgent(yamlContent)` — parse frontmatter from .md, extract `name`, `model` (string, not sub-object), `mode`, `description`, `skills`, `workflows`.

3. **Skill parser rewrite**: Replace `parseSkill(yamlContent)` — parse frontmatter from .md, extract `name`, `description`, `triggers`, `sub_skills`, `canonicality`, `tags`. Body is markdown, not structured YAML.

4. **Workflow parser rewrite**: Replace `parseWorkflow(yamlContent)` — parse frontmatter from .md, extract `name`, `description`, `uses_skills`, `kind`. Body is markdown.

5. **New task parser**: `parseTask(String content, String id)` — extract frontmatter fields. No task parser exists currently.

6. **Changelog parser rewrite**: Replace `parseChangelog()` heading-based parser with frontmatter extraction: `id`, `date`, `project`, `task`, `type`, `impact`, `skills`.

7. **Graph normalizer**: Build `WorkspaceEdge` list from cross-references in frontmatter (agent.skills -> skill, agent.workflows -> workflow, workflow.uses_skills -> skill, task.skills -> skill, task.workflows -> workflow, task.depends_on -> task, changelog.task -> task).

### 9.4 Required model changes (EPIC 03)

1. Add `AssetKind` enum (replace or supplement `AssetType`).
2. Add `EdgeKind` enum (replace freeform string `edgeType`).
3. Add `Canonicality` enum.
4. Add `WorkspaceAsset` class with `frontmatter: Map<String, dynamic>`, `canonicality`, `edges: List<WorkspaceEdge>`.
5. Add `WorkspaceEdge` class with typed `EdgeKind`.
6. Restructure `Agent` to match frontmatter schema (drop `AgentModel`, `AgentTool`, `ToolParameter`, `systemPrompt`, `capabilities`).
7. Restructure `Skill` to match frontmatter schema (drop `SkillInput`, `SkillOutput`, `SkillStep`; add `triggers`, `sub_skills`, `canonicality`).
8. Restructure `Workflow` to match frontmatter schema (drop `WorkflowTrigger`, `WorkflowStage`, `WorkflowErrorHandling`, `RetryPolicy`, `FallbackRule`; add `uses_skills`, `kind`).
9. Restructure `Task` to match frontmatter schema (add `owner`, `skills`, `workflows`, `depends_on`, `proof_state`, `review_score`).
10. Restructure `ChangelogEntry` to match frontmatter schema (add `project`, `task`, `type`, `impact`, `skills`; simplify body).

================================================
FILE: prompt.txt
================================================
You are building a Flutter application prototype called **ASW Observatory**.

The app is a **desktop-first, read-only observability console** for an agentic project workspace. It visualizes a mocked Agent System Workspace containing agents, skills, workflows, tasks, and changelog entries.

You do **not** have access to my real files and you must not ask for them. Instead, create a realistic mock workspace inside the project and build the app around that mock data.

## Non-negotiable execution rule

Before building the actual frontend screens, you must first create a complete **Atomic Design System in Flutter**, then use that design system to build every screen.

Do not hardcode visual styles directly in feature screens. Feature screens must compose tokens, atoms, molecules, organisms, templates, and pages from the design system.

## Visual direction

Look and feel: **ultradark obsidian glass**, with subtle **5% hacker** and **5% protoss** influence.

Interpret this as:

* near-black obsidian background
* glass-like dark panels, but not excessive blur
* subtle cyan/violet/gold energy accents
* thin luminous borders
* precise typography
* dense but readable information architecture
* futuristic, serious, command-center feel
* no childish neon overload
* no generic SaaS pastel dashboard
* no Material default look without customization

Accessibility remains mandatory: readable contrast, keyboard-friendly navigation, visible focus states, and clear semantic status colors.

## Product concept

Build one unified system with four top-level areas:

1. **Map** — what exists and how assets relate.
2. **Operate** — active tasks, lanes, review state, blockers.
3. **History** — changelog timeline and change stories.
4. **Governance** — canonical/generated/archive/provenance/staleness visibility.

The app should show two connected domains:

### A. Harness visibility

Read mocked `.opencode/` data:

```text
.opencode/
  agents/
  skills/
  workflows/
```

Show:

* agents
* skills
* super-skills
* sub-skills
* skill-local workflows
* global workflows
* scripts/references/assets attached to skills
* inter-references between agents, skills, workflows, tasks, and changelog entries

### B. Execution visibility

Read mocked `docs/` data:

```text
docs/
  tasks/
    00-planning/
    01-open/
    02-doing/
    03-review/
    04-completed/
  changelog/
```

Show:

* task lanes
* task detail pages
* changelog timeline
* evidence/readiness/proof status
* links between changelog entries and tasks
* links between tasks and skills/workflows

## Domain model

Model everything as graphable assets.

Create a normalized model similar to:

```dart
enum AssetKind {
  agent,
  skill,
  subskill,
  workflow,
  task,
  changelog,
  script,
  reference,
  rule,
}

enum EdgeKind {
  contains,
  routesTo,
  dependsOn,
  references,
  changedBy,
  proves,
  uses,
}

enum Canonicality {
  parentCanonical,
  childLocal,
  generated,
  appendOnly,
  archive,
  mock,
}

class WorkspaceAsset {
  final String id;
  final AssetKind kind;
  final String name;
  final String path;
  final String description;
  final Canonicality canonicality;
  final Map<String, dynamic> frontmatter;
  final List<String> tags;
  final List<String> triggers;
  final List<WorkspaceEdge> edges;
}
```

Adapt as needed, but keep the idea: one normalized graph backbone powers all screens.

## UX requirements

The app should help users understand:

1. What exists.
2. What matters right now.
3. Why something changed.
4. What is blocked, stale, orphaned, or risky.
5. How agents, skills, workflows, tasks, and changelog entries connect.

Use data storytelling, not just tables.

Examples:

* “This review queue is dominated by code-quality and project-management tasks.”
* “These workflows are global but may belong inside a skill-local workflow folder.”
* “This skill has many incoming references and should be treated as governance-critical.”
* “This changelog entry changed a skill used by three active tasks.”

* central content

Small layout:

* detail view becomes full-screen

## Performance rules

Do not create excessive nested blur/glass effects.

Use glass panels sparingly:

* shell background
* major cards
* selected inspector
* modal/story panels

Avoid making every component a blurred container.

Use lazy lists for catalogs and tasks.

Keep animations subtle and fast.

## Acceptance criteria

The prototype is complete only if:

1. A reusable Flutter Atomic Design System exists.
2. All feature screens use the design system.
3. There is a Design System Gallery route.
4. Mock `.opencode/` and `docs/` workspace files exist.
5. Mock markdown files use valid YAML frontmatter.
6. App loads and visualizes mocked agents, skills, workflows, tasks, and changelog entries.
7. The app has Map, Operate, History, Governance, and Asset Detail surfaces.
8. Task lanes show the five required folders.
9. Changelog timeline links entries to tasks and skills.
10. Skill detail shows subskills, local workflows, scripts/references, and incoming/outgoing links.
11. The app visually matches ultradark obsidian glass with restrained hacker/protoss accents.
12. The app remains readable and accessible.
13. The first implemented milestone must be the design system, not product screens.

## Delivery order

Follow this order strictly:

### Phase 1 — Atomic Design System

Create tokens, atoms, molecules, organisms, templates, and Design System Gallery.

### Phase 2 — Mock Workspace

Create the mock `.opencode/` and `docs/` markdown file corpus with valid frontmatter.

### Phase 3 — Data Layer

Create parsers, models, repositories, and graph normalization.

### Phase 4 — Product Shell

Create navigation, routing, overview dashboard, and layout templates.

### Phase 5 — Feature Screens

Create Map, Operate, History, Governance, and Asset Detail.

### Phase 6 — Polish

Improve responsiveness, story panels, accessibility, visual polish, and demo coherence.

## Important conceptual framing

This is not a generic task manager.

It is an **Agent System Workspace Observatory**.

It should make a governed agentic workspace visible:

```text
agents = institutional roles
skills = routable capabilities
subskills = executable capability units
workflows = operational rites
tasks = governed work contracts
changelog = append-only historical ledger
graph = causality and dependency map
governance = visibility into drift, canonicality, proof, and risk
```

Build the prototype to demonstrate that concept clearly.

# Unified Visibility System for Skills, Workflows, Tasks, and Changelog

## Executive synthesis

Your current harness already behaves less like a loose `.opencode/` folder and more like a governed operating system for agentic work. The imported corpus exposes generated indexes for **38 skills**, **42 agents**, and **43 workflows**, and the updated skills corpus includes a large hierarchical surface with super-skills, sub-skills, skill-local workflows, domain-skills, and interaction-skills. At that scale, a simple file browser or static markdown list will underperform; what you need is a **workspace observatory** that can show hierarchy, cross-references, provenance, and change over time in one place. fileciteturn0file7 fileciteturn0file5 fileciteturn0file6

The most important design conclusion from `harness-architecture` is that skills are not flat documentation assets. The harness uses a **Lobe Gateway** pattern in which a super-skill root acts as an index, while execution knowledge lives in sub-skills and skill-local workflows. It also enforces a stronger governance layer than a normal docs system: ASW scorecards gate new assets, workflows are supposed to live in the narrowest canonical home, and harness-management is explicitly audit-first and read-only by default. That means the frontend should not merely “list files”; it should expose **asset class**, **hierarchy**, **canonical home**, **routing intent**, and **governance status**. fileciteturn0file7

The most important design conclusion from `project-management` is that tasks and changelog are also not generic kanban/wiki artifacts. Recurring work is supposed to become workflows, RF8 is the planning-to-contract layer for complex work, task identity is lane-neutral, `docs/tasks/tasklist.md` is generated rather than manually edited, and `docs/changelog/*.md` is the canonical append-only changelog ledger while `CHANGELOG.md`, `CHANGELOG-FULL.md`, `docs/changelog/index.md`, and per-project views are generated projections. In delegated waves, child agents return evidence, but the parent orchestrator is the single writer for tasklist/changelog/memory closeout. The UI therefore has to distinguish **source-of-truth files** from **generated read models** and should preserve that governance boundary in the interaction design. fileciteturn0file7

My recommendation is to build **one desktop-first Flutter application** that contains two tightly-coupled domains: a **Harness Map** for agents/skills/workflows and an **Execution Ledger** for tasks/changelog. The two should share one data backbone, one graph/search layer, one storytelling layer, and one design system. The result should feel like an “ultradark obsidian glass” observatory, but underneath it should be ruthlessly structured, auditable, keyboard-friendly, and performant. That combination matches both your existing governance model and Flutter’s best-practice architecture guidance around separation of concerns, layered structure, and adaptive UI. fileciteturn0file7 citeturn14view2turn14view3turn12view2turn12view4

## What your current harness implies about the frontend

The frontend should be designed around the rules your skills already encode, not around generic “project management app” assumptions.

First, `harness-architecture` treats the harness as a governed system, not as “a pile of ad-hoc Markdown.” It explicitly says new skills and workflows should pass an ASW scorecard gate, that super-skills use a root index plus sub-skills, that workflow placement should prefer the owning super-skill over global `.opencode/workflows/`, and that child-vs-parent drift should be audited and classified rather than auto-rewritten. `harness-management` also distinguishes parent-canonical assets, child-local overlays, promotion candidates, conflicts, and convergence status. That directly implies the UI needs provenance chips like **parent-canonical**, **child-local**, **promotion candidate**, **conflict**, **same-key-different**, and **workflow-promote-to-skill**, not just tags like “file type.” fileciteturn0file7

Second, `project-management` bakes in a very specific execution worldview. It states that recurring operational patterns should become workflows; RF8 is the upstream planning contract for complex work; task creation should enforce anti-collision numbering and reproducibility-by-design; task references should be lane-neutral; and tasklist/changelog are canonical-via-engine, not manually maintained ledgers. In other words, your task system is less a kanban board and more a **governed evidence pipeline**. The frontend should therefore emphasize **proof**, **dependencies**, **verification commands**, **expected outputs**, **current lane**, **historical lane-at-time**, and **which orchestrator is allowed to publish**. fileciteturn0file7

Third, the agent layer is already operationally rich. The generated agent index shows specialized architect, builder, reviewer, and researcher roles, plus orchestrators like `architect-orchestrator` and `builder-orchestrator`. The index also shows that many agents are disciplinary specialists, not generic assistants. A visibility system should therefore not show “agents” as a flat persona gallery. It should instead show **which assets each agent depends on**, **which workflows each role commonly enters**, and **which skill families dominate the current operating model**. fileciteturn0file5

The practical outcome is that the UI should model four different relationship types at minimum:

| Relationship type | Meaning in your system |
| --- | --- |
| **contains** | super-skill → sub-skill, skill → skill-local workflow |
| **routes-to** | gateway skill → sub-skill or workflow |
| **depends-on** | task/workflow/agent → skill/rule/script/reference |
| **governance-status** | canonical, overlay, promotion candidate, generated, append-only, read-only audit |

That relational model is much closer to your imported files than a naive tree explorer would be. fileciteturn0file7

## The skill and workflow visibility frontend

The skill side should center on a **Harness Map** with three synchronized views: **catalog**, **graph**, and **detail**.

The **catalog view** should break the workspace into top-level tabs for **Skills**, **Agents**, and **Workflows**, with saved filters for families such as super-skills, flat skills, browser-harness domains, orchestration agents, reviewer agents, and generated/global workflows. Because your skills use frontmatter with descriptions, triggers, related skills, sub-skill indexes, and explicit workflow associations, a catalog card can already expose much more than a title: it can show asset class, parent family, trigger density, workflow count, related-skills count, and provenance. That aligns directly with how `harness-architecture` expects new assets to be written and indexed. fileciteturn0file7

The **graph view** should be the differentiator. I would implement three graph modes:

- **Containment graph**: super-skill → sub-skills → local workflows.
- **Operational graph**: agents → primary skills → primary workflows.
- **Governance graph**: parent-canonical vs child-local vs promotion-candidate assets.

This matters because the root `SKILL.md` in the super-skill pattern is intentionally an index, not a full implementation, while sub-skills carry the action knowledge. A graph makes that architecture legible at a glance in a way a folder tree does not. fileciteturn0file7

The **detail view** for a skill should have six panels, all on one screen:

| Panel | What it should show |
| --- | --- |
| **Identity** | name, description, triggers, tags, canonical home |
| **Role in the harness** | gateway, flat execution skill, review harness, provider harness, etc. |
| **Sub-structure** | sub-skills, local workflows, references, scripts |
| **Incoming links** | agents/workflows/other skills that cite or route to it |
| **Operational usage** | common trigger phrases, likely entry workflow, boundary cases |
| **Governance** | scorecard evidence, archive lineage, drift flags, generated-index presence |

That last panel is especially important because your system already distinguishes “what exists” from “what is allowed to mutate.” A good visibility tool should make broken assumptions obvious before they become operational drift. fileciteturn0file7

I would also add a **Pathfinder** feature specifically for “how do I use this thing?” Given any selected skill, the UI should answer: **which agents tend to load it, which workflows mention it, which neighboring skills it routes into, and what evidence or scripts it expects**. That is the exact cognitive gap people hit in a mature harness: not “what files exist,” but “what is the right entry path?” The maturity of your current agent index strongly suggests this will save more time than another static index page. fileciteturn0file5 fileciteturn0file7

A final point: I would keep the initial release strictly **read-only**. That is fully consistent with `harness-management`, which emphasizes audit-first passes and reviewable suggestions rather than blind mutation. Later, if you want managed write actions, the UI should invoke the canonical scripts and workflows rather than directly editing generated or governed surfaces. fileciteturn0file7

## The task and changelog visibility frontend

The task and changelog side should center on an **Execution Ledger** rather than a normal kanban board.

The **task surface** should start with a lane board, because your tasks clearly live in canonical lanes under `docs/tasks/{00-planning,01-open,02-doing,03-review,04-completed}` and `docs/tasks/tasklist.md` is a built projection over those lanes. But the board should not stop at lane columns. Every task card should expose: task number, action type when present, dependency count, verification readiness, last evidence touch, review/fix-loop state, and whether its current lane matches its declared state. That last point is important because the skills explicitly warn against tasks in `03-review/` still declaring active work states. fileciteturn0file7

The **task detail page** should be more forensic than pretty. It should have a header with the lane-neutral identity (`Task NNNN` plus slug), followed by sections for contract, dependencies, validation commands, evidence, and lifecycle. Because `create-tasks` requires exact verification commands, expected semantic outputs, related-task references, and RF8 provenance for complex work, the frontend should parse and elevate those fields instead of burying them in markdown body text. The result should feel closer to a case file than a note. fileciteturn0file7

The **changelog surface** should not be designed as a dumb chronological feed. Your changelog engine explicitly says that `docs/changelog/*.md` is the canonical append-only ledger and that generated views like `CHANGELOG.md`, `CHANGELOG-FULL.md`, `docs/changelog/index.md`, and `docs/changelog/views/<project>.md` are projections. So the UI should preserve two modes: **Ledger mode** for canonical source entries and **Story mode** for grouped, derived narratives by project, milestone, task, or release. That mirrors your own architecture instead of flattening it. fileciteturn0file7

This is where UX research on storytelling becomes valuable. Recent research found that data stories can improve efficiency of comprehension tasks and improve effectiveness for single-insight comprehension compared with conventional visualizations, while DashGuide showed that guided dashboard tours can help users navigate interactions and understand the data model of a dashboard more effectively. For your use case, that means the changelog surface should not simply offer filters; it should offer **guided stories** such as “What changed in harness governance this month?”, “Which tasks clustered around a skill migration?”, and “Why did this review wave expand?” citeturn19academia0turn19academia1

I would therefore implement three changelog views:

| View | Best use |
| --- | --- |
| **Timeline** | exact historical sequence, append-only audit reading |
| **Project story** | per-project generated view with highlights and milestones |
| **Impact story** | change → affected tasks → affected skills/workflows/agents |

The **Impact story** view is the one that makes the whole system feel alive. It connects a changelog entry to the task that motivated it, the workflow that operationalized it, and the skill or harness area it mutated. That is where your project-management model and your harness-architecture model finally meet. fileciteturn0file7

## The best single system for both domains

The best answer to your items two through four is not “two apps with shared styling.” It is one system with two modes over one normalized graph.

I would structure the product as an **ASW Observatory** with four top-level workspaces:

| Workspace | Core question |
| --- | --- |
| **Map** | What exists and how is it related? |
| **Operate** | What work is active, blocked, or ready for review? |
| **History** | What changed, why, and with what proof? |
| **Governance** | What is canonical, generated, local, stale, or risky? |

Under the hood, the observatory should normalize everything into one graph model:

```text
Asset
├─ kind: agent | skill | subskill | workflow | task | changelog | rule | script | reference
├─ path
├─ canonicality: parent-canonical | child-local | generated | append-only | archive
├─ metadata
└─ edges[]
   ├─ contains
   ├─ routes-to
   ├─ depends-on
   ├─ references
   ├─ changed-by
   └─ proves
```

That model matches your actual workspace much better than separate “docs viewer” and “task viewer” apps would. A changelog entry can `changed-by` a task, that task can `depends-on` a workflow, that workflow can `routes-to` a skill, and that skill can be `contains` a sub-skill family. The value here is not just visualization; it is **navigable causality**. fileciteturn0file7

From a workflow point of view, I would release it in three phases.

The **first phase** should be read-only and local. It scans `.opencode/agents`, `.opencode/skills`, `.opencode/workflows`, `docs/tasks`, and `docs/changelog`, builds a normalized index, and exposes search, graph, filters, and storytelling views. No mutation. No write-back. No accidental governance bypass. That is the safest and fastest path to usefulness. fileciteturn0file7

The **second phase** should add guided overlays and analyst features: bookmarks, personal notes, “spotlight tours,” saved graph layouts, and diagnostic views like “orphan workflows,” “skills with no agent affinity,” “tasks referencing stale lane paths,” or “assets with heavy incoming reference load.” Research on dashboard tours and embedded annotations suggests these kinds of guided interpretation layers improve how people navigate complex dashboards and relate findings to one another. citeturn19academia1turn19academia2

The **third phase** can add controlled execution hooks, but only by calling your canonical engines. For example, the UI can expose buttons like **Rebuild tasklist**, **Validate changelog**, **Run ASW audit**, or **Compare child harnesses**, but those actions should shell out to your existing scripts, not synthesize file writes directly. That preserves the governance model you already encoded in the skills. fileciteturn0file7

## Flutter atomic design and UX recommendations

The design system should follow an explicit atomic model, because your domain itself is hierarchical and compositional. Brad Frost’s atomic design frames interfaces as **atoms, molecules, organisms, templates, and pages**, and emphasizes that this is a mental model for understanding both the parts and the whole of a system at once. That maps unusually well onto your workspace because you already think in skill gateways, sub-skills, workflows, and orchestrated surfaces. citeturn24view0

For this app, I would map atomic design like this:

| Atomic layer | In this product |
| --- | --- |
| **Atoms** | typography tokens, icon tokens, status dots, badges, chips, dividers, canonicality colors |
| **Molecules** | searchable filter bars, provenance pills, trigger chips, evidence rows, mini task cards |
| **Organisms** | graph canvas, task lane board, changelog timeline, skill detail panel, guided-tour overlay |
| **Templates** | Harness Map template, Execution Ledger template, Story Mode template |
| **Pages** | concrete project/workspace instances with real content loaded |

That should live on top of Flutter’s theme system. Official Flutter guidance recommends centralizing app-wide styles in `ThemeData`, using `colorScheme` and `textTheme` as primary theme surfaces, and `ThemeExtension` for custom additions to `ThemeData`, typically custom color sets. For your case, `ThemeExtension` is exactly the right place to encode domain semantics such as **parent-canonical**, **child-local**, **promotion candidate**, **generated**, **append-only**, **blocked**, **review**, and **proof-complete** colors. citeturn7view5turn8view0turn9view0

For app architecture, the official Flutter guide recommends separation of concerns with **UI layer** and **Data layer**, further split into views/view models and repositories/services, with an optional domain layer for more complex app logic. It also recommends an MVVM-style one-to-one pairing between views and view models, and stresses well-defined interfaces and boundaries for maintainability, scale, and testability. That is a very strong fit here: use a data layer for file scanning and parsing, a domain layer for graph normalization and narration, and a UI layer for explorers/story views. citeturn14view2turn14view3

For routing and state, I would keep the architecture pragmatic rather than maximalist. Flutter’s own state-management guidance says the right choice depends on app complexity and team preference, and that community packages can reduce boilerplate and support clearer, more consistent architectures. In this specific case, **Riverpod** is a strong fit because the app will juggle async parsing, cached projections, derived filters, and testable separation between logic and UI; **go_router** is a strong fit because it is a declarative router with deep linking, data-driven routes, and `ShellRoute`, and it is published by `flutter.dev`. citeturn14view0turn22view1turn22view0

For the actual component-development workflow, **Widgetbook** is worth adopting early. Its documentation and pub package describe it as a sandbox for building widgets and screens in isolation, mocking hard-to-reach states, cataloging widgets in one place, and—through Widgetbook Cloud—running visual/golden review workflows. For a system where a single detail panel may have dozens of states across skill/task/changelog entities, that is extremely valuable. citeturn15view0turn15view2

For charts and graphing, a practical package stack is:

| Concern | Recommended package | Why it fits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Routing | `go_router` | Declarative URL-based routing, deep linking, nested navigation, and `ShellRoute`; maintained under `flutter.dev`. citeturn22view0 |
| State/data orchestration | `flutter_riverpod` | Separates logic from UI, handles async/error/loading flows cleanly, and is pitched as testable, scalable, and reusable. citeturn22view1 |
| UI sandbox/catalog | `widgetbook` | Isolated widget/screen development, edge-state mocking, shared catalog, golden/visual review support. citeturn15view0turn15view2 |
| Charts | `fl_chart` | Highly customizable charting with line, bar, pie, scatter, and radar support. citeturn23view0 |
| Relationship graph | `graphview` | Supports hierarchical tree layouts, force-directed graphs, Sugiyama layered graphs, and auto-zoom/animation. citeturn23view2turn23view3 |

For adaptive UX, follow Flutter’s current guidance very closely. Flutter’s docs distinguish **responsive** design as fitting the UI into the available space and **adaptive** design as making the UI usable in that space; their best-practices pages recommend breaking down large widgets into smaller ones, not locking orientation, avoiding orientation-based top-level layout switches, not keying layout off device type, and switching navigation patterns such as bottom navigation versus `NavigationRail` according to available space. That maps directly to your product: on narrow widths use a bottom-nav or compact sidebar model; on wide screens use a permanent left rail plus a right-side inspector. citeturn10view4turn12view2turn12view4

For the **look and feel**, I would implement your “ultradark obsidian glass, 5% hacker, 5% protoss” request as a restrained palette rather than a maximal effect stack. Use a near-black base, one cool luminous accent, one warm warning accent, and a semantic status palette. Use glass only on high-value surfaces such as modal inspectors, not everywhere. Flutter’s performance docs warn that `saveLayer()` can be expensive, that opacity and clipping are costly, and that large lists/grids should use lazy builders and avoid unnecessary intrinsic layout passes. In practice, that means: minimal blur, no gratuitous translucent nesting, fixed density rules, lazy list/grid builders, and performance profiling from the start. If you do glassmorphism, do **sparse glassmorphism**. citeturn26view1turn26view2turn26view3

For accessibility, W3C’s WCAG guidance requires at least **4.5:1 contrast** for normal text and **3:1** for large text, and Flutter’s accessibility materials explicitly point to WCAG as a core standard. So even in an ultradark aesthetic, the typography and semantic controls cannot be vague-glow-on-near-black. Your hacker/protoss polish should come from accent edges, subtle motion, and iconography—not from compromising readability. Also ensure complete keyboard navigation, because Flutter’s adaptive guidance calls out keyboard support and accessible navigation as especially important on larger devices. citeturn20view0turn7view7turn12view2

The last UX recommendation is the most domain-specific: treat the product as a **storytelling console**, not just an admin dashboard. Research suggests data stories improve comprehension efficiency, and guided dashboard tours can materially help dashboard users understand interactions and extract insight. For your app, that means every major surface should answer three questions in one screen: **what exists**, **what matters right now**, and **why this changed**. The UI should constantly move users from overview to relationship to evidence. That is the right product shape for a harness this dense. citeturn19academia0turn19academia1

## Open questions and limitations

I can design the frontend direction with high confidence from the imported skills, workflows, and agent indexes, but I did **not** re-parse the full live `docs/tasks/` and `docs/changelog/` corpora in this pass. So the proposed parsers and visual contracts are strong at the governance level, but historical edge cases in older task headers, legacy changelog entries, and project-specific task conventions may still need one validation sweep against the actual live directories before implementation begins. fileciteturn0file7

I would also treat symlinked child-project surfaces as a first-class technical risk. `harness-management` clearly expects parent-canonical reuse, child-local overlays, and convergence audits. The frontend therefore needs safe path-resolution rules and provenance indicators from the first version, otherwise it will mislead you by presenting mirrored files as independent assets. fileciteturn0file7

With those caveats, the core answer is clear: **build one desktop-first Flutter observatory, keep version one read-only, model the workspace as a graph plus ledger, and let the UI reflect your governance doctrine instead of flattening it.** That is the direction most faithful to how your harness already thinks. fileciteturn0file7

# Task 0018 — DS Accessibility Focus Baseline

**Date**: 2026-06-07
**Type**: feature
**Impact**: ds-layer
**Project**: warp-prism

## Summary

Established the minimum accessibility and keyboard-focus baseline for the
Warp Prism design system.

## Changes

- Added Accessibility & Focus States section to Design System Gallery
  demonstrating focus rings, keyboard activation, and semantic labels
- Created `test/design_system/accessibility/design_system_accessibility_test.dart`
  with widget tests for Semantics, focus behavior, and keyboard baseline
- Created `docs/guides/warp-prism-design-system-accessibility.md` documenting
  focus ring rules, contrast ratios, semantic labels, and keyboard activation
  contract for future builders

## Components Covered

- DSChip: focus ring, Enter/Space activation, Semantics (label, button, selected)
- DSFilterChipGroup: focus traversal, individual chip semantics
- DSSidebar: keyboard navigation, button semantics, selected state hints
- DSTopbarAction: focus ring, tooltip semantics, keyboard activation
- DSSearchBar: TextField focus behavior
- DSAssetCard: tappable interaction baseline

## Accessibility Rules Documented

- Focus ring: 2px accentCyan at 50% opacity
- Keyboard: Tab traverses, Enter/Space activates
- Contrast: textPrimary AAA, textSecondary/tertiary AA, status colors AA large
- Disabled: textDisabled color, no tap/focus acceptance

## Why

The app requires one normalized graph shared by Map, Operate, History, and
Governance surfaces. Without a centralized graph builder and edge inference
service, each screen would rebuild relationships independently, leading to
drift and inconsistent truth models.

## Changed

- Created `WorkspaceGraphResult` — the canonical graph return type with
  asset index, edge list, kind grouping, and lookup/query helpers.
- Created `EdgeInferenceService` — pure, stateless edge inference rules
  covering containment, routing, dependency, reference, changed-by, proves,
  and usage relationships.
- Created `WorkspaceGraphBuilder` — single graph build pipeline that takes
  a flat list of `WorkspaceAsset` and returns a normalized `WorkspaceGraphResult`
  with deduplicated typed edges.
- Created barrel export `services.dart` for the data services layer.
- Added comprehensive tests proving graph normalization, edge inference,
  deduplication, and the changelog→task linkage chain.

## Evidence

- `lib/data/services/workspace_graph.dart` — canonical result type
- `lib/data/services/edge_inference_service.dart` — inference rules

# Changelog — Task 0413: Shell States And Deep Link Fallbacks

**Date**: 2026-06-07
**Task**: 0413 — Warp Prism Shell States And Deep Link Fallbacks
**Type**: feature
**Status**: Done

## Summary

Hardened the EPIC-04 shell by implementing shell-level loading, error, empty, and deep-link fallback behavior via `ShellStateHandler`, ensuring the product shell remains truthful and navigable when repositories are empty, parsing fails, or asset-detail routes cannot resolve requested items.

## Files Changed

- **CREATED** `lib/features/shell/shell_state_handler.dart` — `ShellStateHandler` abstract class with static methods:
  - `buildLoading()` / `buildLoadingCompact()` — loading indicators with explanatory messages
  - `buildEmpty()` — empty state with contextual surface name
  - `buildError()` — error state with retry affordance
  - `buildUnresolvedAssetFallback()` — deep-link fallback for unresolved asset IDs
- **CREATED** `lib/features/shell/shell.dart` — barrel export for shell state handler
- **MODIFIED** `lib/app/pages/asset_detail_page.dart` — wired `ShellStateHandler.buildUnresolvedAssetFallback()` for unresolved asset deep links
- **CREATED** `test/features/shell/shell_state_handler_test.dart` — 229 lines covering all four shell states plus deep-link fallback scenarios

## Key Decisions

- Shell states are deliberately distinct: loading ≠ empty ≠ error (no collapsing into one generic placeholder)
- `buildError()` includes a retry affordance for recoverable failures
- Deep-link fallback is a first-class shell concern, not a debug-only edge case
- All methods are static and return `Widget` for inline use in any routed surface without requiring a stateful wrapper

id: 2026-06-07-task-0902-universal-asset-detail-view-model
date: 2026-06-07
project: warp-prism
task: '0902'
type: feature
impact:
  - asset-detail
  - data-model
skills:
  - agent-wiki
---

## Why

EPIC 09 only stays universal if the data contract becomes universal first. Without one shared descriptor, each detail screen would bake its own parsing and section logic, making later variants expensive and inconsistent.

## Changed

- Created `asset_detail_descriptor.dart` (domain) — defines the universal `AssetDetailDescriptor` with shared sections: identity properties, metadata properties, body summary, incoming/outgoing links, related assets, tags, governance diagnostics, and explicit fallback semantics for unsupported kinds.
- Created `asset_detail_mapper.dart` (application) — maps a normalized `WorkspaceAsset` plus its edges into an `AssetDetailDescriptor`. Handles identity section (kind, path, canonicality), metadata section (version, status, priority, lane, model, triggers, dates, custom frontmatter), body summary from description, and incoming/outgoing link derivation from edges. Returns explicit fallback for unsupported kinds (script, reference, rule).
- Created `asset_detail_controller.dart` (application) — exposes `resolveAssetDetail()` as a pure function that takes an asset ID, asset index, edges, and diagnostics, returning an `AssetDetailResult` with resolved/fallback semantics. Also provides `buildAssetIndex()` utility.
- Created test `asset_detail_descriptor_test.dart` covering:
  - Descriptor shared sections for supported kinds (agent, skill, task, changelog)
  - Incoming/outgoing edge derivation with name resolution from asset index
  - Related assets combining incoming + outgoing
  - Unsupported-kind fallback (script kind → explicit fallback)
  - Unknown/empty/"unknown" asset ID fallback
  - Metadata fields: version, status, priority, lane, model, triggers
  - Body summary, tags, governance diagnostics inclusion

## Evidence

- `flutter test test/features/asset_detail/asset_detail_descriptor_test.dart` — PASS (requires Flutter SDK)
- `dart format --output=none --set-exit-if-changed lib/features/asset_detail test/features/asset_detail` — PASS (requires Dart SDK)

# Task 0905 — Responsive Detail Shell Integration

**Date**: 2026-06-07
**Type**: feature
**Scope**: `lib/features/asset_detail/`, `lib/design_system/`, `lib/features/map/`, `lib/features/history/`

## Summary

Integrated the universal asset detail surface into the shell and consumer
workspaces with breakpoint-aware responsive behavior. All workspace surfaces
now delegate detail rendering to a shared `ResponsiveDetailShell` widget
instead of building local inspector layouts.

## What Changed

### New files:
- `lib/features/asset_detail/presentation/responsive_detail_shell.dart`
  — Core responsive wrapper. Renders detail using:
  - **Wide (>= 1200px)**: side-by-side split pane (master left, detail right)
  - **Medium (800-1199px)**: animated overlay drawer from right with scrim
  - **Narrow (< 800px)**: full-screen Scaffold with back arrow in AppBar
- `lib/features/asset_detail/presentation/asset_detail_consumer.dart`
  — Shared consumer wrapper for workspace surfaces. Bridges `selectedAssetId`
  to `ResponsiveDetailShell` with `detailBuilder` callback.
- `lib/features/asset_detail/asset_detail.dart` — Barrel export.
- `test/features/asset_detail/responsive_detail_integration_test.dart`
  — Widget tests for all three breakpoints, open/close/back sync,
  scrim tap, back arrow, breakpoint boundary values, and transitions.

### Modified files:
- `lib/design_system/templates/master_detail_template.dart`
  — Added `onDetailClose`, `detailTitle`, `detailKind` props.
  - Wide: split-pane (unchanged)
  - Medium: overlay drawer with scrim that triggers `onDetailClose`
  - Narrow: full-screen Scaffold with back arrow and `onDetailClose`
- `lib/design_system/organisms/ds_shell.dart`
  — `DSShellResponsive` now supports overlay inspector on medium
  layouts and full-screen inspector on narrow layouts.
  Added `onInspectorClose` callback.
- `lib/features/map/map_workspace_page.dart`
  — Replaced local `Row` layout with `AssetDetailConsumer`.
  Detail now uses responsive behavior across all breakpoints.
- `lib/features/history/presentation/history_page.dart`
  — Replaced hardcoded `MediaQuery` width check with
  `ResponsiveDetailShell`. Detail now responds to all breakpoints
  with proper close/back behavior.

## Behavioral Contract

- `onDetailClose` / `onInspectorClose` fires on ALL breakpoints:
  - Wide: via the `DSDetailInspector` close button in the detail header
  - Medium: via scrim tap or `DSDetailInspector` close button
  - Narrow: via back arrow in AppBar or `DSDetailInspector` close button
- Consumer surfaces must clear their selection state in response.
- No device-type names; all branching is width-based via `DSBreakpoints`.

# Task 1010 — Accessibility Contrast and Focus Pass

## What changed
- Raised `textTertiary` from `#606070` to `#8888A0` in `ds_colors.dart` for WCAG AA compliance (~6.0:1 on obsidianDeep)
- Raised `textDisabled` from `#404050` to `#505060` (disabled text exempt from WCAG but improved baseline)
- Added keyboard focus support (FocusNode, Enter/Space activation, visible focus ring) to:
  - `_SidebarItemWidget` in `ds_sidebar.dart`
  - `DSTopbarAction` in `ds_topbar.dart`
  - `DSChip` in `ds_chip.dart`
  - `DSTaskCard` in `ds_task_card.dart`
  - `_FilterChip` in `ds_filter_chip_group.dart`
  - `DSLinkRow` in `ds_detail_inspector.dart`
- Added `Semantics` wrappers to all interactive and structural components:
  - `DSSidebar`, `_SidebarItemWidget`, `_DefaultHeader`
  - `DSTopbar`, `_Breadcrumbs`, `DSTopbarAction`
  - `DSChip`, `DSTaskCard`, `_PriorityBadge`, `_ReviewScore`
  - `DSFilterChipGroup`, `_FilterChip`
  - `DSText` (all variants wrapped with Semantics, optional `semanticsLabel` override)
  - `DSDetailInspector`, `_InspectorHeader`, `_InspectorSection`, `DSPropertyRow`, `DSLinkRow`
  - `DSLaneBoard`, `_LaneColumn`, `_LaneHeader`, `_EmptyLane`
- All focus indicators use cyan ring: `DSColors.accentCyan.withOpacity(0.5)` with 2px width
- All interactive elements show `DSColors.obsidianActive` background on keyboard focus

## Why
The obsidian dark theme had textTertiary at #606070 which yielded only 2.7:1 contrast ratio on
obsidianDeep (#050508), failing WCAG AA for normal text (requires 4.5:1). All interactive
components relied solely on mouse hover with no keyboard activation path, making the design
system unusable for keyboard-only navigation and screen readers.

## Test coverage
- `test/design_system/accessibility_focus_contrast_test.dart` — verifies contrast ratios,
  color distinctness, token integrity, and focus indicator visibility

# Task 1020 — Responsive Shell and Detail Pass

## What changed
- Created `ds_breakpoints.dart` token class with centralized breakpoint constants:
  - `narrow` (600px): below this, sidebar hidden and search bar collapses
  - `sidebarCollapse` (800px): sidebar switches between expanded and collapsed
  - `timelineDetail` (1000px): timeline switches between inline and side-by-side detail
  - `masterDetailSideBySide` (1200px): master-detail switches between overlay and side-by-side
- Exported `DSBreakpoints` from `tokens.dart` barrel
- Updated `DSShellResponsive` in `ds_shell.dart` to use `DSBreakpoints` instead of hardcoded values
  - Added narrow (<600px) behavior: hides sidebar entirely
  - Documented width contract in class docstring
- Updated `master_detail_template.dart` to use `DSBreakpoints` for all responsive decisions:
  - `MasterDetailTemplate`: uses `masterDetailSideBySide` and `sidebarCollapse`
  - `TimelineTemplate`: uses `timelineDetail`
- Updated `DSTopbar` in `ds_topbar.dart`:
  - Search bar now collapses below `DSBreakpoints.narrow` (600px) width
  - Search uses `ConstrainedBox(maxWidth: 300)` instead of fixed `SizedBox(width: 300)`
  - Breadcrumbs wrapped in Expanded to prevent overflow
- Documented responsive contract with docstrings on `DSShellResponsive` and templates

## Why
Breakpoints were scattered and duplicated across 3+ files with hardcoded pixel values.
The topbar search bar was fixed at 300px with no collapse behavior, causing overflow on
narrow screens. There was no breakpoint below 800px, meaning the sidebar would still
render on very narrow viewports. A centralized `DSBreakpoints` class ensures all responsive
decisions reference a single source of truth.

## Test coverage
- `test/design_system/responsive_shell_test.dart` — verifies breakpoint values, ordering,
  spacing between ranges, and layout token constants

# Task 1030 — Empty, Loading, and Error State Coherence

## What changed
- Created shared `DSStateSurface` molecule with `empty`, `loading`, and `error` constructors
- Replaced ad-hoc `_EmptyLane` in `ds_lane_board.dart` with `DSStateSurface.empty`
- Replaced ad-hoc `_EmptyTimeline` in `ds_timeline.dart` with `DSStateSurface.empty`
- Added empty-state guard to `ds_graph_canvas.dart` when nodes list is empty
- Added empty-state guard to `ds_detail_inspector.dart` when sections list is empty
- Added empty-state guard to `ds_story_panel.dart` when insights list is empty
- Exported `ds_state_surface.dart` from molecules barrel
- Created regression test `test/design_system/state_surface_test.dart`

## Why
The observatory had inconsistent state handling: one organism showed "No tasks" with an icon,
another showed "No changelog entries" with different layout, and graph/inspector/story surfaces
had no state handling at all. A shared contract ensures users can always distinguish
"no data yet" from "loading" from "something broke."

# Task 1040 — Glass Performance Budget Pass

## What changed
- Created performance budget report at `docs/reports/epic-10-glass-performance-budget.md`
- Audited all 40 design system files for BackdropFilter/blur usage
- Documented surface classification: narrative, detail, cards, board, graph, shell, modal
- Codified 6 rules for blur usage (default-is-simple, no nesting, no blur on scrollables, etc.)
- Created regression test `test/design_system/glass_budget_test.dart`
- Verified no host requires surgical swap — codebase was already disciplined

## Why
The research brief explicitly calls for "sparse glassmorphism." Without a documented budget,
new glass surfaces can proliferate silently into high-frequency list/board hosts where blur
is most expensive. The budget codifies the current disciplined state and prevents regression.

## Key finding
Only 1 of ~15 host surfaces uses BackdropFilter blur: `DSStoryPanel` (elevated, sigma 15).
All other surfaces use `DSGlassPanelSimple` or plain `Container`. No surgical swaps needed.

# EPIC 10 — Observatory Demo Walkthrough Script

> **Status**: v1.0 — narrative contract
> **Generated**: 2026-06-07 by Task 1050
> **Purpose**: Single-source walkthrough that ties EPIC 10 acceptance questions to real file-backed surfaces
> **Blocked surfaces**: Marked with ⛔ — no page/route exists yet; narrative contract is ready but host is absent.

---

## Narrative Spine

The demo answers five questions in order. Each question maps to a workspace, a host surface, and a `DSStoryPanel` instance.

| # | Question | Workspace | Host Surface | Status |
|---|----------|-----------|-------------|--------|
| 1 | What exists? | Map | Graph canvas + asset catalog | ⛔ No page |
| 2 | What matters now? | Operate | Lane board + task detail | ⛔ No page |
| 3 | Why did this change? | History | Timeline + changelog story | ⛔ No page |
| 4 | What is risky? | Governance | Diagnostic surface + provenance | ⛔ No page |
| 5 | How do assets connect? | Map (graph) | Relationship graph + pathfinder | ⛔ No page |

### Anti-Hallucination Note

No live page, route, or app shell exists for any workspace. The narrative contract below describes what each surface **should** host once a page is created. The `DSStoryPanel` component and its enhanced `DSStoryNarrativeInsight` model are file-backed and testable without a running app.

---

## Beat 1 — Map: "What exists?"

**Core question**: How many agents, skills, workflows, and tasks are in the workspace?

**Story panel configuration**:
```
DSStoryPanel(
  title: 'Workspace Map',
  subtitle: 'What exists in the ASW Observatory',
  icon: Icons.map_outlined,
  accentColor: DSColors.accentCyan,
  insights: [
    DSStoryNarrativeInsight(
      text: '38 skills across 13 families',
      detail: '12 super-skills, 26 sub-skills',
      value: '38',
      evidence: 'assets/mock_workspace/.opencode/skills/',
      riskLevel: InsightRiskLevel.none,
      connection: 'harness-architecture governs all skill families',
    ),
    DSStoryNarrativeInsight(
      text: '9 specialized agents with distinct roles',
      detail: '3 orchestrators, 6 domain specialists',
      value: '9',
      evidence: 'assets/mock_workspace/.opencode/agents/',
      riskLevel: InsightRiskLevel.none,
      connection: 'agents → skills via uses edges',
    ),
    DSStoryNarrativeInsight(
      text: '42 workflows across review, build, and governance',
      detail: 'global workflows + skill-local workflows',
      value: '42',
      evidence: 'assets/mock_workspace/.opencode/workflows/',
      riskLevel: InsightRiskLevel.low,
      connection: 'workflows → skills via dependsOn edges',
    ),
  ],
)
```

**Fallback**: If graph canvas has not been implemented, show `DSStoryPanel` alone with an explanatory footer noting the graph is blocked.

```
    ),
    DSStoryNarrativeInsight(
      text: 'Changelog entries link back to motivating tasks',
      detail: 'changedBy edge type connects changelog → task',
      evidence: 'lib/data/models/changelog_contracts.dart',
      riskLevel: InsightRiskLevel.none,
      connection: 'Impact story view connects change → task → workflow → skill',
    ),
    DSStoryNarrativeInsight(
      text: 'Governance status is modeled as provenance',
      detail: '6 canonicality values: parentCanonical, childLocal, generated, appendOnly, archive, mock',
      evidence: 'lib/data/models/workspace_graph.dart',
      riskLevel: InsightRiskLevel.none,
      connection: 'DSColors.forCanonicity() maps provenance to color tokens',
    ),
  ],
)
```

---

## Narrative Contract Summary

The `DSStoryPanel` + `DSStoryNarrativeInsight` contract supports four required narrative layers:

| Layer | Field | Purpose |
|-------|-------|---------|
| **Insight** | `text`, `value`, `color` | What the data says |
| **Evidence** | `evidence` (file path or URL) | Where to verify the claim |
| **Risk** | `riskLevel` (none/low/medium/high/critical) | How dangerous the gap is |
| **Connection** | `connection` | How this insight relates to other assets or blocks |

This contract is testable without a running app: the model classes validate structurally, and the `DSStoryPanel` widget renders them via `flutter_test` widget tests.

---

## Workspace-to-Question Mapping

| Workspace | Questions Answered | Primary Surface | Secondary Surface |
|-----------|-------------------|-----------------|-------------------|
| Map | What exists? How do assets relate? | Graph canvas | Asset catalog |
| Operate | What matters now? | Lane board | Task detail |
| History | Why did this change? | Timeline | Changelog story |
| Governance | What is risky? What is stale? | Diagnostic panel | Provenance pills |

---

## Fallback Notes

1. **No app shell**: All beats are currently document-only. `DSStoryPanel` can be tested as a widget but cannot be navigated to.
2. **No Flutter SDK**: Validation commands (`flutter analyze`, `flutter test`) are blocked. Narrative contract is exercised via unit/widget tests once SDK is available.
3. **No pages directory**: All four workspaces (Map, Operate, History, Governance) lack page implementations. The narrative contract is page-independent.
4. **Legacy models.dart**: Still imports Flutter; new code targets `data_models.dart` barrel. No conflict for narrative work.

# Warp Prism Design System — Accessibility Baseline

> Task 0018 — Established 2026-06-07

## Purpose

This document defines the minimum accessibility and keyboard-focus baseline
for the Warp Prism design system.  All feature screens built on top of the
DS must inherit these rules — do not retrofit accessibility in page code.

---

## 1. Focus Ring

Every interactive DS component uses a **consistent focus indicator**:

| Property       | Value                                        |
|----------------|----------------------------------------------|
| Border width   | `2px`                                        |
| Border color   | `DSColors.accentCyan.withOpacity(0.5)`       |
| Trigger        | Keyboard focus (Tab / Shift+Tab)             |
| Animation      | `DSMotion.fast` on border width/color change |

Components with this baseline:
- `DSChip` (all interactive variants)
- `DSFilterChipGroup` → `_FilterChip`
- `DSSidebar` → `_SidebarItemWidget`
- `DSTopbarAction`
- `DSSearchBar` (TextField border changes on focus)

---

## 2. Keyboard Activation

All tappable interactive components respond to:

- **Enter** — activates the component
- **Space** — activates the component

This is implemented via `Focus.onKeyEvent` + `KeyDownEvent` checks in each
interactive widget.  Tab order follows the widget tree order.

---

## 3. Semantic Labels

| Component           | Semantics Property | Value                          |
|---------------------|--------------------|--------------------------------|
| `DSChip`            | `label`            | Chip label text                |
| `DSChip`            | `button`           | `true` when interactive        |
| `DSChip`            | `selected`         | Current selection state        |
| `DSFilterChipGroup` | `label`            | `"Filter options"`             |
| `_FilterChip`       | `label`            | Option label                   |
| `_FilterChip`       | `button`           | `true`                         |
| `DSSidebar`         | `label`            | `"Navigation sidebar"`         |
| `_SidebarItemWidget`| `label`            | Item label text                |
| `_SidebarItemWidget`| `hint`             | `"Currently selected"` or `"Double-tap to navigate"` |
| `DSTopbar`          | `label`            | `"Top navigation bar"`         |
| `DSTopbarAction`    | `label`            | Tooltip text or `"Action button"` |
| `DSTopbarAction`    | `button`           | `true`                         |
| `_Breadcrumbs`      | `label`            | `"Breadcrumb navigation: ..."` |

---

## 4. Contrast Rules

All text/background pairs must meet WCAG AA minimum:

| Pair                         | Ratio Required | Level  |
|------------------------------|----------------|--------|
| `textPrimary` on `obsidianDeep`  | ≥ 7.0:1      | AAA    |
| `textSecondary` on `obsidianDeep`| ≥ 4.5:1      | AA     |
| `textTertiary` on `obsidianDeep` | ≥ 4.5:1      | AA     |
| `textTertiary` on `obsidianBase` | ≥ 4.5:1      | AA     |
| Status colors on `obsidianDeep`  | ≥ 3.0:1      | AA lg  |

Verified by: `test/design_system/accessibility_focus_contrast_test.dart`

---

## 5. Status Colors

Semantic status colors are distinct and meet WCAG AA large text minimum:

| Token            | Usage                    |
|------------------|--------------------------|
| `statusSuccess`  | Completed, healthy       |
| `statusWarning`  | Attention needed         |
| `statusError`    | Failure, blocked         |
| `statusInfo`     | Neutral information      |

---

## 6. Disabled State

Disabled components:
- Use `DSColors.textDisabled` for text and icons
- Do **not** respond to `onTap` or keyboard activation
- Do **not** receive keyboard focus (when `enabled: false`)

---

## 7. Known Limitations

- **Asset cards**: `DSAssetCard` does not yet have explicit `Semantics` wrapping
  or `Focus`/`onKeyEvent`.  It relies on `GestureDetector` only.  This is an
  acceptable gap for v0.1.0 since cards are demonstrated read-only in the gallery
  but will need focus support when interactive in product screens.
- **Search bar icons**: The clear and filter `_IconButton` sub-widgets use
  `InkWell` which provides Material ripple but not explicit `Semantics`.  When
  product screens add real search, these should get `Semantics(label:)` and
  `Tooltip`.

---

## 8. Testing

- **Contrast tests**: `test/design_system/accessibility_focus_contrast_test.dart`
  — WCAG ratio calculations on all text/background pairs
- **Focus & semantics tests**: `test/design_system/accessibility/design_system_accessibility_test.dart`
  — Widget tests verifying Semantics tree and keyboard baseline

---

## 9. Gallery Demonstration

The **Accessibility & Focus States** section in the Design System Gallery
(`lib/design_system/gallery/design_system_gallery_sections.dart`) provides
a live visual proof of:

- Focus ring pattern description
- Focusable chips with keyboard activation
- Filter chip group with selection states
- Sidebar navigation with focusable items
- Topbar action buttons with focus states
- Semantic status colors
- Contrast rules summary

# Feature Catalog: Gap — Multimodal Endpoints

> **Series**: 1400
> **EPICs**: EPIC-1400 (Multimodal Endpoint Framework), EPIC-1410 (Image Generation), EPIC-1420 (Audio Endpoints), EPIC-1430 (Video & Music Generation), EPIC-1440 (Moderation & Rerank), EPIC-1450 (Batch Processing)
> **Gap Source**: diegosouza-omniroute (image gen, audio, video, music, moderation, rerank, batch endpoints)
> **Total Features**: 50

## Gap Analysis Summary

Our catalog currently defines domain types for image generation (`KindImageGen`, `KindAudio`) and skeleton OpenAI endpoints (`776`, `777`, `778`) at P2 priority, but lacks:
- Full multimodal endpoint framework with provider routing
- Video generation endpoints
- Music generation endpoints
- Content moderation endpoint
- Reranking endpoint
- Batch processing API
- File operations API for batch inputs
- Relay endpoint for cross-model hand-off

These are significant gaps. The diegosouza reference supports 22 image gen providers, 10 STT providers, 15 TTS providers, 11 video gen providers, 5 music gen providers, and 6 reranking providers.

## Classification Guide

- **CORE**: Image generation, audio (TTS/STT), moderation, rerank — needed for a complete OpenAI-compatible gateway
- **EXTENDED**: Video generation, music generation, batch processing — valuable but not essential for v1
- **ECOSYSTEM**: Relay endpoint, niche multimodal features

---

## Features

### Multimodal Endpoint Framework (1400-1409)

| # | Name | Description | Classification | Priority | Proposed EPIC |
|---|------|-------------|---------------|----------|---------------|
| 1400 | Multimodal Provider Interface | Define `MultimodalProvider` interface: `GenerateImage(ctx, req)`, `Transcribe(ctx, req)`, `Synthesize(ctx, req)`, `Moderate(ctx, req)`, `Rerank(ctx, req)` — unified interface for non-LLM capabilities | CORE | P1 | EPIC-1400 |
| 1401 | Multimodal Request/Response Models | Define unified request/response models for each multimodal type: image gen request (prompt, size, quality, n), audio request (file, language, format), rerank request (query, documents, model) | CORE | P1 | EPIC-1400 |
| 1402 | Multimodal Workload Classification | Extend workload classifier for multimodal requests: `WorkloadKindImageGen`, `WorkloadKindAudioSTT`, `WorkloadKindAudioTTS`, `WorkloadKindVideoGen`, `WorkloadKindRerank`, `WorkloadKindModeration` | CORE | P1 | EPIC-1400 |

# Feature Catalog: Gap — Advanced Routing Strategies

> **Series**: 1500
> **EPICs**: EPIC-1500 (Advanced Load Balancing), EPIC-1510 (Intelligent Routing), EPIC-1520 (Specialized Routers), EPIC-1530 (Multi-Factor Auto Routing)
> **Gap Source**: diegosouza-omniroute (priority, context-relay, fill-first, P2C, random, least-used, reset-aware, auto scoring, LKGP, intent classifier, task-aware, deprecation router, wildcard router, tag router, eval-based, pipeline router)
> **Total Features**: 40

## Gap Analysis Summary

Our catalog covers core routing strategies (weighted round-robin, least-connections, least-latency, random weighted, hash-based affinity, capacity-aware, cost-aware, health-weighted) in Series 630-639 and pluggable strategies in 670-675. However, the diegosouza reference implements ~20 additional routing strategies that represent meaningful capability gaps:

1. **Priority-based routing** — simple but essential, not explicitly in our catalog
2. **Quota/reset-aware routing** — routes based on quota windows, not just capacity
3. **Context relay** — cross-model session handoff (novel)
4. **Multi-factor auto scoring** — composite scoring with sub-strategy combination
5. **Intent/task classification** — intelligent routing based on request semantics
6. **Model management routers** — deprecation routing, model family fallback, wildcard matching
7. **Pipeline routing** — multi-step sequential model chains (partially covered by 629)

Many of these extend rather than replace existing EPIC-630/640/650/670 features.

## Classification Guide

- **CORE**: Priority routing, quota-aware routing, LKGP, model deprecation routing, wildcard routing — essential for production gateway
- **EXTENDED**: Auto scoring, intent classifier, task-aware, context relay, pipeline routing — valuable for intelligent routing
- **ECOSYSTEM**: Eval-based routing, tag router — nice-to-have, niche

---

## Features

### Advanced Load Balancing Strategies (1500-1509)

| # | Name | Description | Classification | Priority | Proposed EPIC |
|---|------|-------------|---------------|----------|---------------|
| 1500 | Priority Routing | Implement ordered priority routing: iterate providers in explicit priority order, first available wins; simpler than weighted for strict preference ordering | CORE | P1 | EPIC-1500 (new) or extend EPIC-630 |
| 1501 | Fill-First Routing | Implement fill-first load balancing: maximize usage on primary provider before moving to next; fill quota on preferred provider before spilling over | CORE | P1 | EPIC-1500 |
| 1502 | Power of Two Choices (P2C) | Implement P2C load balancing: randomly pick two candidates, select the less loaded one; O(1) with good distribution | EXTENDED | P2 | EPIC-1500 |
| 1503 | Least-Used Routing | Implement least-used routing: route to provider with lowest total historical usage in current period; differs from least-connections (current vs cumulative) | CORE | P1 | EPIC-1500 |
| 1504 | True Random Routing | Implement strict random routing without fallback weighting: uniform distribution, useful for A/B testing and load distribution experiments | EXTENDED | P2 | EPIC-1500 |
| 1505 | Reset-Aware Routing | Implement reset-aware routing: consider provider quota reset windows; prefer providers whose quotas reset soonest (use capacity about to expire) | CORE | P1 | EPIC-1500 |
| 1506 | Reset-Window Ordering | Implement reset-window ordering: sort providers by quota reset timestamp, route to provider with nearest reset to maximize utilization before reset | CORE | P1 | EPIC-1500 |
| 1507 | LKGP (Last Known Good Provider) | Implement LKGP routing: track last provider that returned a successful response for this workload type; prefer it for subsequent requests; fast recovery after transient failures | CORE | P1 | EPIC-1500 |
| 1508 | Emergency Fallback Provider | Implement emergency fallback: configure a last-resort stable provider (e.g., free tier) that activates only when all primary/secondary providers are down | CORE | P1 | EPIC-1500 |
| 1509 | Strategy Composition | Support composing multiple strategies: primary strategy + tiebreaker strategy + emergency fallback; configurable per route graph node | EXTENDED | P2 | EPIC-1500 |

# Feature Catalog: Gap — Prompt Compression & Context Management

> **Series**: 1600
> **EPICs**: EPIC-1600 (Context Manager), EPIC-1610 (Compression Pipeline), EPIC-1620 (Thinking Budget)
> **Gap Source**: diegosouza-omniroute (7-mode compression pipeline, context manager, thinking budget, progressive aging)
> **Total Features**: 35

## Gap Analysis Summary

Our catalog has no features related to prompt compression, context window management, or thinking token budgets. The diegosouza reference implements a sophisticated 7-mode compression pipeline (off/lite/standard/aggressive/ultra/rtk/stacked) with progressive message aging, caveman compression (semantic condensation), and rule-based tool output compression. This is a significant gap — context management is essential for cost optimization and handling large conversations.

Key gaps:
- **Context window management** — enforcing model context limits, token estimation
- **Prompt compression** — reducing token count while preserving semantics
- **Progressive aging** — older messages get progressively compressed
- **Thinking budget** — allocating reasoning tokens for thinking models (o1, Claude extended thinking)
- **Tool output truncation** — compressing verbose tool results
- **System prompt deduplication** — eliminating repeated system prompt content

## Classification Guide

- **CORE**: Context manager, token estimation, basic compression, thinking budget — essential for production use
- **EXTENDED**: Advanced compression modes, progressive aging, caveman compression — valuable optimization
- **ECOSYSTEM**: Ultra compression with external SLM, language packs for caveman compression

---

## Features

### Context Manager (1600-1609)

# Feature Catalog: Gap — Guardrails & Safety

> **Series**: 1700
> **EPICs**: EPIC-1700 (Prompt Injection Guard), EPIC-1710 (PII Protection), EPIC-1720 (Tool Calling Policy), EPIC-1730 (Vision Bridge), EPIC-1740 (Response Safety)
> **Gap Source**: diegosouza-omniroute (prompt injection guard, PII masker/sanitizer, vision bridge, tool calling policy, response sanitizer)
> **Total Features**: 35

## Gap Analysis Summary

Our catalog defines a `Guardrail` domain type (15D), a `GuardrailEvaluator` interface (168), and plugin-based guardrails (1250-1254) including content filter, PII detection, and injection detection. However, the existing features are primarily at the plugin/interface level and lack:

- **Concrete prompt injection detection** with multiple modes (warn/block/redact)
- **PII masking/sanitizer** for both input AND output with pattern-specific handling
- **Vision bridge** — bridging image inputs for non-vision providers
- **Tool calling policy** — allowlist/denylist/disabled per exposure/model
- **Response sanitizer** — post-call output sanitization pipeline
- **Guardrail metrics and audit** — detailed tracking of guardrail decisions

The diegosouza reference has production-level implementations of these features, not just interfaces.

## Classification Guide

- **CORE**: Prompt injection guard, PII protection, tool calling policy — critical for security
- **EXTENDED**: Vision bridge, response sanitizer, advanced PII techniques
- **ECOSYSTEM**: Custom guardrail marketplace

---

## Features

### Prompt Injection Guard (1700-1709)

| # | Name | Description | Classification | Priority | Proposed EPIC |
|---|------|-------------|---------------|----------|---------------|
| 1700 | Injection Detection Engine | Implement prompt injection detection: pattern matching against known injection techniques, scoring system, confidence threshold | CORE | P1 | EPIC-1700 (new) |
| 1701 | Injection Detection Patterns | Maintain injection pattern database: system prompt override attempts, role confusion, instruction ignoring, delimiter injection, encoding attacks | CORE | P1 | EPIC-1700 |
| 1702 | Injection Mode: Warn | Warn mode: detect potential injection, log warning, add `x-injection-warning` header, allow request through | CORE | P1 | EPIC-1700 |
| 1703 | Injection Mode: Block | Block mode: detect injection above threshold, reject request with 400 error, log blocked attempt with details | CORE | P1 | EPIC-1700 |
